ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 2 — Focused Visit (Follow-up) — Elvis Presley — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: One-week review, seen the same day by addiction medicine: diagnoses, buprenorphine started in the office, the benzodiazepines combined into one, the sleep study and home blood pressure results

text.paragraph: One-week review, seen the same day by addiction medicine. [S]

Mr. Presley returns one week after intake and is seen by Dr. Eberhardt-Mensah of addiction medicine on the same day. He has taken only the medicines this clinic prescribed, from one pharmacy, and brought the remaining tablets. As agreed, he took his last hydromorphone about 18 hours ago and his last oxycodone about 20 hours ago so that buprenorphine could be started today; he has yawning, a runny nose, aching legs, gooseflesh and loose stools. He took his usual diazepam and alprazolam last night. His in-laboratory sleep study three days ago showed moderate obstructive sleep apnea. His home blood pressure readings over six days, after stopping phentermine, averaged 146/94. His bowels opened twice this week on polyethylene glycol and senna. He has kept his firearms locked and the naloxone in the house. He says he is ready to start treatment before his engagement. [S]

list.item:
Opioid use disorder, severe (F11.20). Dr. Eberhardt-Mensah confirms opioid use disorder, severe, with seven DSM-5-TR criteria: more taken than intended, unsuccessful efforts to cut down, much time spent getting prescriptions from several prescribers, craving, continued use despite sleepiness and constipation, tolerance and withdrawal (counted because the opioids were not taken as prescribed). Buprenorphine is the treatment of choice; taking a benzodiazepine is not a reason to withhold it, but the combination calls for naloxone, a single prescriber and close follow-up. COWS 12 today, so buprenorphine was started in the office: 4 mg, then 4 mg after an hour, with withdrawal settling. [S]
Buprenorphine with naloxone 16 mg tomorrow and daily after that.
Full-agonist opioids stopped; remaining tablets taken back.
Weekly phone or video contact for the first month; counseling started.
Naloxone continued.

Benzodiazepine use disorder, moderate (F13.20). Five criteria met; daily diazepam and alprazolam for years mean a risk of seizures if stopped quickly. The two benzodiazepines are combined into diazepam alone, a long-acting drug, at 40 mg a day, a cautious equivalent of his combined doses, and held there until buprenorphine is stable. [S]
Diazepam 10 mg four times daily; alprazolam stopped.
Taper by about 5 to 10% every two to four weeks once buprenorphine is stable, starting at the next visit if he is ready.
CBT for anxiety and insomnia.

Obstructive sleep apnea, moderate (G47.33). Moderate obstructive sleep apnea, with a small central component that opioids and benzodiazepines can worsen; CPAP at 11 cm H2O controlled events in the titration. [S]
CPAP nightly, with a travel machine.
No sedative added for sleep.

Hypertension, stage 2 (I10). A home average of 146/94 a week after stopping phentermine confirms stage 2 hypertension, more than 10 mmHg above the diastolic target, so two first-line drugs are started together. Today's office reading is raised further by withdrawal. [S]
Amlodipine 5 mg with valsartan 160 mg once daily.
Potassium and creatinine in two to four weeks.
Home readings twice daily for a week before the next visit.

Opioid-induced constipation (K59.03). Meets Rome IV criteria for opioid-induced constipation; buprenorphine usually constipates less than full agonists. [S]
Continue polyethylene glycol and senna.

Fatigue, weight gain, constipation, sleepiness and high blood pressure (R53.83). Explained by the diagnoses made today; this presenting problem is closed. [S]
Followed under each diagnosis.

text.paragraph: Guideline basis: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain — United States, 2022 (2022); The ASAM National Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder: 2020 Focused Update (2020); Joint Clinical Practice Guideline on Benzodiazepine Tapering: Considerations When Risks Outweigh Benefits (2025); Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs (PDMPs) (2026); 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); Treatment of Adult Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Positive Airway Pressure: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline (2019); American Gastroenterological Association Institute Guideline on the Medical Management of Opioid-Induced Constipation (2019); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024)

Follow-up: Phone check tomorrow and weekly contact. Three-week review. Call or use naloxone and 911 for heavy sedation or slow breathing. Next scheduled visit 1974-08-07: three-week review on buprenorphine: withdrawal and cravings, the first benzodiazepine taper step, blood pressure treatment, CPAP, constipation and weight, and planning for a Las Vegas engagement. [S]
